table.title: The effect of feedback and experience on human operators’ reliance and trust during AFRS-assisted one-to-one face matching tasks
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Research Question: Does feedback or experience increase human reliance on the simulated AFRS decision-aid in a one-to-one face matching task?

H1: The aided performance of all three conditions will fail to reach the level of performance achieved by the AFRS alone (replicating Carragher & Hancock, 2023; Carragher et al., 2023). 

H2: Aided performance on the main face matching task will be influenced by level of training, with greater performance following the feedback condition compared to the experience condition, and greater performance following the experience condition compared to the control condition. 

H3: Relative trust in the AFRS will be influenced by level of training. Specifically, relative trust will be higher following the feedback condition compared to the experience condition, and higher following the experience condition compared to the control condition. 
H4: Relative trust in the AFRS will be positively associated with aided performance on the face-matching task.

H5: Relative trust in the AFRS will be positively associated with reliance on the AFRS. 

H6: Reliance on the AFRS will be positively associated with aided performance on the face-matching task. 

H7: Reliance on the AFRS will be influenced by level of training, with greater reliance following the feedback condition compared to the experience condition, and greater reliance following the experience condition compared to the control condition. However, the relationship between level of training and reliance on the AFRS will be mediated by relative trust in the AFRS.
table.design_dependent_variables:
On each trial of the short Kent Face Matching Test (KFMT: Fysh & Bindemann, 2018), participants will be asked to decide whether two simultaneously presented faces show the same person. Participants will respond to the question “Do these photographs show the same person, or two different people?” along a 6AFC scale, which contains an identification decision (same, different) and an associated level of confidence (definitely, probably, guess).  These 6AFC responses will be used to calculate all possible measures of performance on the face matching task. We will report overall accuracy [((Hits + Correct Rejections) / Total Trials)*100)] in the main text, to ensure that these data are easily understood by all readers. However, we can also use these responses to calculate measures from signal detection theory, including Area Under the Curve (AUC), sensitivity, or criterion (Macmillan & Creelman, 2004; Stanislaw & Todorov, 1999). If reported at all, these other measures of performance would likely be placed in the supplementary materials.

Our other key measure will be that of reliance. Here we define reliance as instances in which the participant changes their final response to be more alike that of the AFRS. We anticipate measuring reliance in steps of confidence change. The identification responses are made on a 6-point scale from “Definitely Same” to “Definitely Different” (1-6). However, we will create a measure of reliance in which the participant’s initial decision becomes point 0, and the final decision is calculated in units of confidence change, with positive values indicating the decision becoming more alike the AFRS and negative units demonstrating “rejection” (in which the final decision moves away from the decision of the AFRS). An alternative measure of reliance is that of binary identification change (i.e., did the participant change from a “same” identification decision to a “different” identification). However, this measure does not capture the more nuanced changes in confidence that can still be attributed to AFRS reliance (i.e., moving from “guess same” to “probably same”). Reliance on the AFRS is not possible when participants make an initial decision that matches that of the AFRS with “definite” confidence (i.e., the participant’s initial decision is “Definitely same”, and the AFRS also shows “same”). We will remove these trials from the calculation of reliance measures, and report them separately (since it is still possible, though unusual, for the participant to show “rejection” of the system’s decision in these cases, which would occur if their final decision moved away from that of the system after it confirmed their initial decision).

Trust in the AFRS will be measured using Lee and Moray’s (1994) two item relative trust in automation measure. As in their original study, we will subtract self-confidence ratings from trust in automation ratings, to leave a change score in which positive values indicate higher relative trust in the automated system and negative values greater self-confidence. In addition to Lee and Moray’s established measure, we will also ask participants whether they trust the AFRS to help them in the task (binary “yes” or “no”), and to give estimates (0-100%) of their individual accuracy, the accuracy of the AFRS, and their accuracy when assisted by the AFRS. Any exploratory analyses will be clearly identified as such in the resulting text.
table.study_design_overview: The experiment has a mixed measures design. Training Condition (feedback, experience, control) will be a between-participants factor. Participants in the “feedback” condition will complete the training trials with the AFRS and receive feedback on the correct answer to each trial in this block. Participants in the “experience” condition will also complete the training trials with the AFRS, but will not receive feedback. Participants in the “control” condition will complete the training trials, but without the AFRS (i.e., they are only making independent decisions), and without receiving feedback. Decision Phase (initial, assisted) will be a within-participants factor in the main face matching task.
table.statistical_tests:
General Principles
	Where appropriate, all inferential tests will be reported with standardised effect sizes (such as "η" _"p" ^"2" ) and 95% confidence intervals. Significant interactions in ANOVA analyses will be interpreted using simple main effects. If necessary, the significance threshold for multiple comparisons will be adjusted via the Bonferroni method of correction. Frequentist analyses (specifically, t-tests/simple main effects) might be supplemented with equivalent Bayesian analyses, which can be used to provide evidence in favour of the alternative (H1) or null (H0) hypotheses. As in Carragher and Hancock (2023), we would report Bayes Factors testing the alternative hypothesis (BF10). All analyses will likely be conducted using JASP/JAMOVI statistical software, with default priors set for Bayesian analyses.

Trust Measures
	Participants will be asked to complete the trust measures three times in the experiment (pre-training, post-training, post-KFMT). Comparisons between trust in automation and self-confidence ratings collected pre-training and post-training will be crucial for testing our hypotheses about the effect of experience and feedback on trust in automation and self-confidence (H3). However, we will use the responses to trust questions collected post-training (i.e., before participants complete the main KFMT) when investigating whether relative trust in automation is related to measures of overall accuracy and reliance (H4, H5, H7). These post-training measures reflect the participant’s intention to trust/distrust the system immediately before the main task. We will also collect responses to the same questions post-KFMT (i.e., after completing the main face matching test), so that we can continue monitoring how trust in automation and self-confidence change with experience using the AFRS. 

Planned Analyses

H1: We will use three one sample t-tests to compare the level of aided performance achieved by each Feedback Condition (feedback, experience, control) in the aided task phase with the level of performance achieved by the AFRS alone (overall accuracy = 95.0%). 

H2: We will use a mixed measures ANOVA with Decision Phase (initial, assisted) as a within-participants factor and Training Condition (feedback, experience, control) as a between-participants factor to examine whether any increase in face matching performance in the main task is related to feedback or experience during the training block. 

H3: We will use a mixed ANOVA with Task Phase (pre-training, post-training) as a within-participants factor and Feedback Condition (feedback, experience, control) to investigate the change in relative trust in automation following the training block. 

H4: We will use a Pearson’s correlation to examine the association between relative trust post-training and performance during the aided phase of the task. 

H5: We will use a Pearson’s correlation to examine the association between relative trust post-training and reliance on the AFRS during the aided phase. 

H6: We will use a Pearson’s correlation to examine the association between reliance on the AFRS and performance during the aided phase of the task.

H7: We will use a mediation analysis (PROCESS macro, Model 4) with Training Condition (feedback, experience, control) as the predictor variable, relative trust post-training as the mediator variable, and performance during the aided phase of the task as the outcome variable.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Our exclusion criteria will be very similar to those used previously (Carragher & Hancock, 2023; Carragher et al., 2023). In the current study, data will be excluded from participants who attempt the face matching task more than once, as well as those who complete the study too quickly (< 8 minutes *subject to revision) or too slowly (> 60 minutes *subject to revision). All data will be excluded from participants who fail an attention check face matching trial).
table.sample_size:
All data collection will occur online. Participants will be recruited from the research platform Prolific (www.prolific.co.uk). Participants will be eligible to complete the study if they are USA nationals currently living in the USA, are 18 years of age or older, and are fluent in English. We will also include screening criteria based on previous performance on Prolific, such that participants will only be eligible for the current study if they have participated in at least 5 previous experiments on Prolific, have a minimum accepted completion rate of 95%, and have not previously participated in any other study conducted by Dr Carragher on Prolific. By design participants will not be able to complete the experiment on a mobile device. 

Our choice of sample size is based on an estimated medium sized interaction of "η" _"p" ^"2"  = .06, on the measure of overall accuracy with the factors of Training Condition (feedback, experience, control) and Decision Phase (initial, assisted). An a priori power analysis (G*Power: Faul et al., 2009), with recommended effect size specifications, indicated that 156 participants (total) would be required to achieve 80% power to detect an interaction effect of "η" _"p" ^"2"  = .06 in a 3 x 2 mixed ANOVA with an alpha set at .05. As such, we will aim to recruit 210 participants, which should leave us with data from approximately 180 participants in total (~60 per training condition), once our exclusion criteria have been applied.
table.additional_comments:
Method
Kent Face Matching Test (KFMT): All participants will complete the short version of the KFMT (Fysh & Bindemann, 2018). The short KFMT consists of 40 unfamiliar face pairs (20 identity matches, 20 identity mismatches). The stimuli will be presented in colour, and the presentation order of all trials will be random. 

Face Matching Trial Procedure: Two faces will be presented onscreen simultaneously. The question shown on each trial will be “Do these photographs show the same person, or two different people?”. Participants will give a 6AFC response which consists of an identification decision (“same” or “different”) and a confidence (“definitely”, “probably”, “guess”). Participants will first give their unassisted independent decision to each trial. Once the initial response has been made, two new sentences will appear below the original question prompt. The first will show participants their initial response (as a reminder). Below that will be the sentence “Facial Recognition System Says:…” with the possible responses being “SAME” and “DIFFERENT”. For the purpose of calculating reliance, these decisions will be treated as “Definite” from the AFRS. Participants will then be asked to make their final judgment, again using the 6AFC response options.

Attention Check: As in our previous work (Carragher & Hancock, 2023; Carragher et al., 2022), we will insert an attention check trial into the main face matching task. The attention check trial will be a mismatched pairs of famous faces that, even if not familiar to the participant, can be correctly resolved by differences in ethnicity. Data from participants who fail to correctly respond “different” (at any level of confidence) to the attention check trial will be discarded from all analyses. The AFRS will not show a decision for the attention check shown – rather, the system will report that it is “OFFLINE”.

AFRS: As in Carragher and Hancock (2023), the decisions made by the simulated AFRS in the experiment will be based on the performance of the real Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN). In the current study, this was a research DCNN from Imperial College London shared with PJBH. This DCNN computes a similarity score between the two faces, which it evaluates against a threshold value to make a final identity decision (see Carragher & Hancock, 2020, 2023). 
The real DCNN correctly resolved 40/40 trials in the short KFMT (overall accuracy 100%). To achieve our desired level of performance for the simulated AFRS (see below), we selected two face pairs that the simulated AFRS would be seen to err on in the experiment (one match pair, one mismatch pair). The selected trials were those that received the similarity values closest to the real system’s decision threshold (i.e., those that were closest to being errors). 
In this study, the simulated AFRS will err on the same two pairs (one match trial, and one mismatch trial) for all participants, which gives the AFRS an overall accuracy of 95% (sensitivity of d´ = 3.29). However, participants will only be told that the facial recognition system is “highly accurate” and “state-of-the-art” (unlike our previous experiments, in which participants were told the accuracy of the system directly).
Since the average performance of humans on the short KFMT is 66% (Fysh & Bindemann, 2018), an AFRS with an overall accuracy of 95% is likely to benefit most participants. 

Measures of Trust: Relative trust in the AFRS will be measured using Lee and Moray’s (1994) two item relative trust in automation measure. As in the original study, we will subtract self-confidence ratings from trust in automation ratings, to leave a change score in which positive values indicate higher trust in the automated system and negative values greater self-confidence. In addition to Lee and Moray’s established measure, we will also ask participants whether they trust the AFRS to help them in the task (binary “yes” or “no”), and to give estimates (0-100%) of their individual accuracy, the accuracy of the AFRS, and their accuracy when assisted by the AFRS (see Additional Documentation). 
Participants will complete the trust questions three times; initially before completing the training block (pre-training), after the training block but before the main task (post-training), and then again after the main experiment (post-KFMT). 
We will conduct our planned analyses based on participant’s responses to the post-training relative trust measure, since this represents the intention of the participants to trust the system immediately prior to the main face matching task. However, we anticipate conducting exploratory analyses to investigate how trust in the AFRS might change after using the system as a decision aid (i.e., from post-training to post-KFMT).

Training Trials (Feedback & Experience Manipulation): Before starting the main face matching task (KFMT), all participants will complete 20 training trials (simply presented to participants as the “first face matching task”). Those in the feedback condition will interact with the AFRS and see the correct answer after each trial. This feedback can be used by the participants to see whether they or the AFRS provided the correct answer. Participants in the experience condition will complete the training trials with the AFRS, but will not receive feedback. Participants in the control condition will complete the training trials, but without the AFRS and without feedback. The 20 training trials will come from the unfamiliar faces of the Stirling Famous Face Matching Test (Carragher & Hancock, 2020). The AFRS will be seen to make 1 error over the 20 trials, giving it an accuracy of 95% (just like the main experiment). The error trial will be selected in the same way as for the main experiment (i.e., that with the similarity rating closes to the real DCNNs decision threshold). Participants then responded to the question “was your final decision correct or incorrect?” to reinforce the feedback.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. live_data_statements: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three training conditions: feedback (AFR system, trial-by-trial feedback), experience (AFR system, no feedback), or control (no AFR system, no feedback).

Less is known about perceptions of AFR systems in these tasks, although public opinion about facial recognition technologies varies widely (Ritchie et al., 2021). Howard et al. (2020) reported participants were more inclined to trust themselves to make face matching decisions, compared to algorithms or other people.

Therefore, we included a third control condition in which participants completed the training block without feedback or the AFR system, which allowed us to isolate the contribution of AFR system experience from mere exposure to an unfamiliar face matching task.
All participants were recruited online through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/).

Participants were eligible for the study if they were U.S.A. nationals living in the U.S.A., at least 18 years old, self-declared English fluency, and had participated in at least 5 previous experiments on Prolific with a minimum approval rate of 95%.
A total of 226 individuals provided informed consent to participate.
Participants were told that the facial recognition system in the experiment was "highly accurate" and "state-of-the-art" but were not explicitly told the accuracy of the system.

Before the main KFMT, all participants completed the first face matching task, which consisted of 20 trials from the unfamiliar section of the Stirling Famous Face Matching Test (SFFMT: Carragher & Hancock, 2020).

Participants completed the trust questionnaire three times; before the training block (pre-training), after the training block but before the main task (post-training), and then again after the main experiment (post-KFMT).
Participants were told that they would be completing two face matching tasks, and that they would be using a simulated AFR system at times in the experiment.
As a reminder, participants were told that the simulated AFR system was "state-of-the-art" and would be "highly accurate" but not exactly how accurate it would be.
Participants completed the trust questionnaire three times (pre-training, post-training, post-KFMT).

As in past research, our participants were untrained novices, probably with little to no experience of performing face matching comparisons or using AFR systems (Carragher & Hancock, 2023; Carragher et al., 2024; Hua et al., 2026; Mueller et al., 2026).
All participants gave informed consent prior to participation.

text.text: Identity verification often involves deciding whether two images show the same person or two different people.

Automated Facial Recognition (AFR) systems can improve unfamiliar face matching accuracy when used as decision aids, yet humans consistently fail to use them optimally, with average automation-assisted performance regularly below that of the system alone.
This suboptimal performance may reflect participants' difficulty in appropriately weighing their trust in the automation with self-confidence in their own ability.

We investigated whether a brief training block with either trial-by-trial feedback, or simple exposure to the AFR system, would improve automation-assisted unfamiliar face matching performance in a subsequent task.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three training conditions: feedback (AFR system, trial-by-trial feedback), experience (AFR system, no feedback), or control (no AFR system, no feedback).

While we found all conditions improved with assistance from the AFR system in the subsequent face matching task, the feedback condition improved significantly more than the experience and control conditions.
Feedback specifically increased trust in automation, which led to greater reliance on the AFR system.
However, greater reliance also led to greater acceptance of rare AFR system errors in the feedback condition.

Our results show that a brief period of trial-by-trial feedback, but not mere exposure to the AFR system, can improve automation-assisted unfamiliar face matching performance, offering a promising direction for improving identification outcomes.

text.text: The aim of the current study was to investigate whether we could improve automation-assisted unfamiliar face matching performance.
We tested whether providing trial-by-trial feedback during an initial "training block" would increase reliance on the AFR system in a subsequent automation-assisted unfamiliar face matching task.

We expected that trial-by-trial feedback would assist participants in gauging the performance of the AFR system (i.e., that it is highly accurate), and of their own ability (i.e., that they are probably less accurate than the AFR system).
These conditions should lead to increases in RTIA, which in turn, should lead to greater reliance on the AFR system in the subsequent task.
A second "experience" condition completed the training block with the AFR system, but without receiving trial-by-trial feedback.

The experience condition was included to test whether explicit feedback was necessary for improved automation-assisted performance or whether participants could make inferences about levels of performance simply from completing the initial task with the AFR system (i.e., Carragher & Hancock, 2023).

text.text: Therefore, we included a third control condition in which participants completed the training block without feedback or the AFR system, which allowed us to isolate the contribution of AFR system experience from mere exposure to an unfamiliar face matching task.
Based on the literature reviewed above, we preregistered the following hypotheses 1.
The aided performance of all three training conditions will fail to reach the level of performance achieved by the AFR system alone.

H2: Aided performance on the main face matching task will differ as a function of training condition, with the feedback condition showing greater performance than the experience condition, and the experience condition showing greater performance than the control condition.

H3: Relative trust in the AFR system will differ as a function of training condition.
Specifically, relative trust will be higher following the feedback condition compared to the experience condition, and higher following the experience condition compared to the control condition.
H4: Relative trust in the AFR system will be positively correlated with aided performance on the main face matching task.

H7: Relative trust in the AFR system will mediate the effect of training condition on aided performance.

Specifically, we expect training to increase relative trust most following the feedback condition, followed by the experience condition, then the control condition, and that higher relative trust will in turn produce greater aided performance on the main face matching task.

text.text: A total of 226 individuals provided informed consent to participate.

We removed data from 3 participants who did not start the face matching task, 17 who did not complete the experiment on their first attempt, and 2 who failed an attention check face matching trial (see below).
Given our sample size, we did not exclude participants based on their experiment completion time.

In total, our analysis consisted of 204 participants: 68 in the control condition (Mage = 41.6, SD = 13.5; 47 female, 19 male, 2 non-binary), 68 in the experience condition (Mage = 41.6, SD = 14.1; 35 female, 30 male, 2 non-binary, 1 non-disclosed), and 68 in the feedback condition (Mage = 38.4, SD = 13.6; 31 female, 36 male, 1 non-binary).
The experiment consisted of two unfamiliar face matching tasks.
However, the first task served solely to deliver the key feedback and experience manipulation (referred to as the "training block" in this manuscript, but not to participants).
The second "main" task was where we investigated whether the feedback or experience manipulation affected AFR system use.
All analyses reported below come from performance on this second task.
The main experiment had a mixed measures design.
Training Condition (feedback, experience, control) was a between-participants factor.
Decision Phase (initial, assisted) was a within-participants factor.
All participants made an initial unassisted identification decision to each trial, before seeing the prediction of the simulated AFR system, and then making a final assisted decision.
The main task used the short version of the Kent Face Matching Test (KFMT: Fysh & Bindemann, 2018b), which consists of 40 pairs of unfamiliar faces (20 identity matches, 20 identity mismatches).

text.text: The short KFMT is a challenging unfamiliar face matching task, with normed average overall accuracy of 66% (Fysh & Bindemann, 2018b).

text.text: The stimuli were presented in the original test format: in colour, and with one image smaller than the other (as it was from a student ID card).
The 40 trials were presented in random order, within a single trial block.
The two faces were presented onscreen simultaneously, with the question "Do these photographs show the same person, or two different people?"
shown below.
Responses were made on a 6-point scale, consisting of an identification decision ("same" or "different") and a level of confidence ("definitely", "probably", "guess").
First, participants made their unassisted initial decision on the trial.
Once the initial response was made, two new lines appeared below the original question prompt.
The first reminded participants of their initial response, while the second said "Facial Recognition System Says:…" with the possible responses being "SAME" and "DIFFERENT".
Participants then made their final assisted response to the trial, using the same response options.
The predictions of the simulated AFR system in the experiment were based on the performance of a real DCNN on the same face matching taskfoot_0 .

Overall Accuracy.
We calculated overall accuracy according to the formula ((Hits +
Correct Rejections) / Total Trials)*100, where hits were correct "same" responses to match trials and correct rejections were correct "different" responses to mismatch trials.
Our primary interest was whether the training conditions differed in their subsequent use of the AFR system.

As such, significant interactions in ANOVAs are often interpreted by comparing the change in performance achieved by each condition (final accuracy -initial accuracy), which also removed any baseline differences in initial accuracy between the conditions.
Overall accuracy does not include decision confidence.
Area Under the Curve.

We calculated Area Under the Curve (AUC) to characterise participants' ability to discriminate between identity match trials and mismatch trials at different response thresholds (Macmillan & Creelman, 2004; Stanislaw & Todorov, 1999).
text.formatted: We calculated Area Under the Curve (AUC) to characterise participants' ability to discriminate between identity match trials and mismatch trials at different response thresholds <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Macmillan & Creelman, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Stanislaw & Todorov, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: AUC is calculated by plotting a participant's hit rate against their false alarm rate (incorrectly responding "same" to a mismatch trial) at each level of the response scale to produce a Receiver Operator Characteristic (ROC) curve.
The measure AUC has a maximum value of 1.0, a minimum of 0.0, and 0.5 indicates chance responding.
Our preregistration described analysing automation "reliance", which we define as occurring when participants change their initial decision to become more like that of the AFR system.
However, it is also possible, albeit very rare (see exploratory results), for participants to "reject" the AFR system's prediction.

Because we have included all trials in our analysis of decision change (deviating from our preregistration), rather than focusing only on reliance, we now use "automation use" as the superordinate term for decision changes following the AFR system's prediction (even though most decision changes are examples of reliance).
We report two measures of automation use: steps of confidence scale change, and changes in binary identification decisions.
All identification responses were made on a 6-point scale from "Definitely Same" to "Definitely Different" (numeric values 1-6).
AFR system outputs were treated as being of "definite" confidence.

To calculate confidence change, the participant's initial decision became point 0, and their final decision was transformed into units of confidence scale change, where positive values show "reliance" as the decision moved toward that of the AFR system (e.g., an initial "guess same" response that changes to "probably same" after the AFR system predicts "same" is +1 units), and negative units show "rejection" (the final decision moved away from the AFR system).
These analyses use average scale change across all trials (including those where the final response did not differ from the initial response).

We also report binary identification decision change, which occurred only when the underlying identification decision changed from initial to final response (changing from "same" to "different", or vice versa).

Our primary measure from this questionnaire was RTIA, which was calculated by subtracting self-confidence ratings from trust in automation ratings (Carragher et al., 2024; Lee & Moray, 1994).

We investigated whether the provision of trial-by-trial feedback, or simple experience using the simulated AFR system, during an initial "training block" could improve automation-assisted performance in a subsequent unfamiliar face matching task.
Across all three conditions, the AFR system proved to be a useful decision aid, such that assisted performance was significantly better than the accuracy participants achieved on their own.
Despite the significant improvements, all three conditions used the decision aid suboptimally, failing to achieve the level of accuracy the AFR system offered alone.
Both results replicate past findings (Bartlett et al., 2024; Carragher & Hancock, 2023; Carragher et al., 2024; Hua et al., 2026; Mueller et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Both results replicate past findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bartlett et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Carragher & Hancock, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Carragher et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Hua et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Mueller et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: With that overarching constraint noted, we found participants who received trial-by-trial feedback in the training block recorded a larger increase in automation-assisted performance compared to participants in the experience and control conditions.

Importantly, the feedback was delivered on a different set of faces, and at a different point in time (prior to the main task), speaking to the generalised nature of the improvement offered by the intervention.
To the best of our knowledge, these are the first results to show that the use of an automated decision aid can be improved in an unfamiliar face matching task.

We had expected that the provision of feedback during the training block would help participants to gauge both their own unfamiliar face matching ability, and the capabilities of the AFR system, which in turn would lead to greater reliance on the AFR system in the main task and increased automation-assisted performance.
Our results were consistent with this mechanism.
The feedback condition showed a large increase in relative trust in automation (RTIA) following the training block.
Separate analysis of self-confidence and trust in automation, the two ratings that contribute to RTIA, showed that their increase in RTIA was due to a significant increase in trust in automation.
There was a small decrease in their selfconfidence, which was consistent across all conditions.
Our exploratory analyses showed that this increase in trust in automation, and RTIA, was maintained through the experiment.

Building on previous research (Carragher et al., 2024), which showed a positive relationship between RTIA and automation-assisted performance, here we show that an intervention that increases trust in the AFR system can also improve automation-assisted performance.
text.formatted: Building on previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Carragher et al., 2024)</ref>, which showed a positive relationship between RTIA and automation-assisted performance, here we show that an intervention that increases trust in the AFR system can also improve automation-assisted performance.

text.text: Our mediation analysis offered partial support for RTIA as the mechanism underlying the feedback condition's advantage.
Their larger increase in aided performance compared to the experience condition was partly explained by their higher post-training RTIA, consistent with the account above.
However, their advantage over the control condition was not mediated by RTIA.

This asymmetry is interpretable in light of our exploratory analyses: the control condition's RTIA also increased (non-significantly), but because of a decline in self-confidence as opposed to an increase in trust in automation.
Because RTIA is a change score, it offers an incomplete description of the factor feedback influenced.

What distinguished the increase in RTIA for the feedback condition was specifically an increase in trust in automation, and it is that component, rather than the composite change score measure, that appears to drive improved automation use.

Our predictions that the experience condition would benefit more from the training block the control condition, which we expected to manifest as increased automation-assisted performance, were unsupported.

Although previous research reported evidence consistent with participants gauging the reliability of the AFR system through exposure (Carragher & Hancock, 2023), other lines of unfamiliar face matching research show that individual performance does not improve through repeated exposure to the task (Bindemann et al., 2012; Carragher & Hancock, 2025), including for professionals (White et al., 2014).

text.text: Crucially, this null result is also consistent with a recent study, showing that automationassisted unfamiliar face matching performance does not improve with time over the course of a task (Carragher et al., Under Review).

text.text: Taken together, these results suggest that explicit feedback is needed to improve automation-assisted performance, rather than experience alone.
Across all participants, we found that RTIA was positively correlated with automation-assisted performance (regardless of performance measure).
Those who had greater trust in automation relative to their self-confidence in their own abilities improved more when using the AFR as a decision aid.

It is important to remember that at 95% accuracy, the simulated AFR system far exceeded the performance of the average participant on the KFMT (Fysh & Bindemann, 2018b), so greater trust in automation was generally appropriate.

text.text: All three conditions did have a positive RTIA value pre-training, though of approximately just 0.5 units of the 10-point scale, which underestimated the 30% advantage of the AFR system compared the initial response accuracy.

These findings replicate previous research, with similar medium-large effect sizes (Carragher et al., 2024), further highlighting RTIA as an important factor in understanding the use of decision aids (Dzindolet et al., 2003; Lee & Moray, 1994; Lee & See, 2004), including in the context of unfamiliar face matching performance.

text.text: We asked participants to make an initial unassisted and final assisted decision on every trial (Hua et al., 2026; Mueller et al., 2026), which allowed us to measure direct instances of AFR system reliance, unlike past research on face matching and trust in automation (Carragher et al., 2024).

text.text: With this new method, we found that RTIA was positively correlated with greater use of the AFR system, whether use was measured as the magnitude of response change toward the system's output, or as the frequency of binary identification decisions changes.
We also showed greater use of the AFR system was associated with greater automation-assisted performance.

While these later findings are not particularly surprising (i.e., that using the highly accurate system more often would lead to better assisted performance), they offer a sensible grounding of our results.

Though our planned analyses showed these relationships were evident in correlations across the entire sample, our exploratory analyses showed that the feedback condition also displayed greater use of the AFR system compared to the experience or control conditions, consistent with their increased RTIA and overall improved automation-assisted accuracy.
While we refer to automation use throughout this project, our exploratory analyses showed that 97.9% of identification decision changes were examples of reliance on the automation.
However, our data show that this increase in automation-assisted performance was not without cost to the feedback condition.
While rare AFR system errors were detrimental to all conditions, the decrease in accuracy was greater for the feedback condition than the experience or control conditions.

Thus, increasing reliance on the AFR system was effective overall for the feedback condition, since the accuracy of the AFR system was greater than the average operator, and following the advice led to endorsing many more correct answers.
But following the system more often, perhaps uncritically, appears to have led the feedback condition to endorse more errors that the other two conditions.

This pattern of results was previously hinted at in the data of Hua et al. (2026), with increased acceptance of algorithm errors under conditions that promoted greater reliance on the algorithm (increased time pressure).

text.text: One of the reasons given for human involvement in the deployment of AFR systems is for detecting and correcting algorithm errors.
Our current findings highlight the inherent difficulty of this task.
Among our novice participants, most would benefit from following the AFR system more often than they already do (since they show suboptimal performance, H1).
But always following the system means that rare errors are less likely to be corrected.

As in past research, our participants were untrained novices, probably with little to no experience of performing face matching comparisons or using AFR systems (Carragher & Hancock, 2023; Carragher et al., 2024; Hua et al., 2026; Mueller et al., 2026).

text.text: Further research is still needed with experienced users of AFR systems to ensure the generalisability of these findings.

But our findings also show that simply getting experience using the AFR system in the training block did not lead to any additional improvement in performance beyond the control condition (see also Carragher et al. Under Review).

text.text: We also acknowledge that while our findings show feedback improved automation-assisted performance, it was to a level of performance below that of the AFR system alone, just like the experience and control conditions.
Nonetheless, this increase in automation-assisted occurred after only 20 trials of feedback in the training block.

An obvious direction for future research is to investigate whether a longer training block with more opportunities for feedback could lead to more substantial improvements in automation-assisted performance.
Despite these limitations, our findings offer promising directions for future research, having shown that it is possible to improve human use of the AFR system in an unfamiliar face matching task.
As facial recognition technologies improve, AFR systems will become more prevalent in applied settings.

But these systems are typically used by, or under the supervision of, a human operator, so advances in technological capability will not automatically translate into improved outcomes; outcomes will depend on how effectively human operators use these systems (Noyes & Hill, 2021).

text.text: Previous research has shown that novice participants struggle to use AFR systems effectively as decision aids (Bartlett et al., 2024; Carragher & Hancock, 2023; Carragher et al., 2024; Hua et al., 2026; Mueller et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown that novice participants struggle to use AFR systems effectively as decision aids <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bartlett et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Carragher & Hancock, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Carragher et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Hua et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Mueller et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Here we show, for the first time, that this use can be improved.

A brief training block of trial-by-trial feedback (20 trials, on a different set of faces, before the task of interest) increased trust in the AFR system, increased reliance on it, and improved automation-assisted accuracy in a challenging unfamiliar face matching task.
That such a light-touch and transferable intervention produced a measurable benefit is an encouraging sign for the development of future approaches to operator training.

Effective use is not the same as uncritical reliance, however, and our results are a reminder that interventions which increase reliance may also reduce the detection of the rare system errors that human oversight is meant to catch.

Calibrating the trade-off between greater reliance on the AFR system when it is correct, but greater rejection of the system when it is incorrect, is the central challenge for future work in the field of automation-assisted unfamiliar face matching.
